To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) T(reg) cells inhibit the migration of pathogenic T cells into CNS; (2) the effect occurs within the secondary lymph nodes and is not mediated by the direct effect on the effector cells; and (3) the therapeutic effect may be due to the reduced expression of the T cell homing receptor CXCR- 3.
the activation and polyclonal expansion of T(reg)-cells in the secondary lymphatic organs interfered with the migration of encephalogenic T cells into target organs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction of T(reg)s and effector T cells and how they affect each other.
the role of T-regulatory cells in the treatment of autoimmune diseases such as multiple sclerosis.
the role of Treg in autoimmune diseases, in particular multiple sclerosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the expansion of polyclonal CD4+ CD2S+ T-regulatory cells interferes with the infiltration of effector cells into the CNS by preventing their migration through the lymph nodes and spleen.
T(reg) are able to prevent the infiltration of the CNS in EAE by inhibiting the transmigration of effector T cells in the secondary organs and by reducing the secretion of IFN-γ in the CNS.
the polyclonal expansion of T(reg)s in the periphery interfered with the migration of effector cells to the CNS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
polyclonal expansion of regulatory cells interferes with the migration of effector cells into the target tissue.
polyclonal expansion of regulatory CD4+ CD28+ T cells in the periphery is instrumental to prevent the migration of encephalogenic T cells into CNS.
Treg cells are important in controlling autoimmuny in the CNS.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the therapeutic effects of polyclonal activation and expansion of regulatory T (Treg) cells in experimental autoimmune encephalyitis (EAE) is achieved by inhibition of encephalogenic T cell infiltration into the central nervous system (CNS) within the secondary lymphatic organs, despite the absence of regulatory T cells in the spinal cords.
T(reg) cell therapy may be a useful approach for the treatment and/or prevention of MS and that the effects are mediated by the inhibition of the migration of pathogenic T cells into CNS.
polyclonal expansion of T(reg)-cells in secondary lymphoid organs may be sufficient to control encephalitogenesis, at least in the rat model of EAE.
